consensus_summary: The horse primarily symbolizes war, military power, and conquest; the white horse specifically symbolizes victorious conquest. Rev 19’s rider is settled as the returning Christ; Rev 6:2’s crowned bow-bearing rider is conquest whose identity is disputed (Christ/gospel advance, Antichrist/counterfeit, or generic/imperial militarism), with Zechariah’s colored horses as background agents of divine purpose.
book_summary: The white horse is the mount of an executing spirit; the conqueror who wins the nations by the covenant bow (tied to Rev 6:2).
consensus_core_identification: Victorious conquest (white = victory/righteousness), rider of Rev 6:2 disputed among divine/gospel, counterfeit, or impersonal military agents
book_core_identification: Mount of an executing spirit; conqueror who wins the nations by the covenant bow
boundary_disagreement: Book keeps the conquest referent for the Rev 6:2 white horse but narrows the open rider debate to one precise identity (executing spirit using a covenant bow to win nations), thereby excluding the common Antichrist/counterfeit and purely human-militarism options and omitting the settled Rev 19 Christological case plus the general horse-as-false-military-hope motif.
rationale: Minimum cores both center on the white horse of Rev 6:2 as conquest/conqueror. Consensus leaves the rider’s identity open across several well-attested readings while treating conquest itself as the stable category; the book preserves that category yet materially tightens its extension and precision by stipulating an ‘executing spirit’ mounted and conquering nations via a ‘covenant bow.’ This rejects some consensus-admitted cases without replacing the central conquest referent, yielding refinement rather than divergence or novelty.
strongest_objection: ‘Executing spirit’ and ‘covenant bow’ are not stated in Rev 6:2 nor listed as such among consensus alternatives, so the narrowing may import an unshared technical construct rather than merely selecting inside the existing debate.
